name: Bear Spirit (Shona)
description: The Bear Spirit of Shona tradition represents the integration of bear symbolism into the rich spiritual landscape of the Shona people of Zimbabwe, where traditional animal totems and spirit hierarchies have adapted to include this powerful northern creature. While the Shona homeland in southern Africa has no native bear species, the Shona spiritual system is built around a complex hierarchy of ancestral spirits known as mhodzi and vadzimu, along with animal totems called mitupo that connect clan lineages to specific animal powers. In this framework, the bear spirit has been incorporated as a symbol of strength, protection, and healing power that transcends geographical boundaries. The Shona concept of unifying the physical and spiritual worlds through animal mediators allows for the recognition of bear power even in regions where bears do not naturally occur, reflecting the dynamic and adaptive nature of African traditional spirituality in an increasingly interconnected world
source: Regional survey of Southern African Bantu oral traditions and folklore — Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Sotho, and related peoples as documented by Bleek, Callaway, Junod, and ethnographic records from the 19th–20th centuries.

name: Bear Water-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: The Bear Water-Spirit of Cheyenne tradition is closely associated with Bear Butte, known in Cheyenne as Noahvose or The Sacred Mountain Where They Are Taught, which rises from the plains of South Dakota as a sacred landmark of immense spiritual significance. In Cheyenne cosmology, the bear is a powerful guardian of springs and water sources, and the mountain itself is shaped like a sleeping bear, guarding the waters that emerge from its base. The Cheyenne prophet Sweet Medicine, Motseyuef, received the four Sacred Arrows from the Maiyun spirits inside Bear Butte after spending four years in a sacred cave whose entrance was guarded by a grizzly bear and a mountain lion. This water-spirit aspect of the bear connects the life-giving springs that emerge from Bear Butte with the spiritual teachings that form the foundation of Cheyenne culture, law, and ceremonial life. The bear water-spirit ensures that the waters of the sacred mountain remain pure and accessible for all who come to pray and seek visions
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Bear Water-Spirit of Muisca
description: The Bear Water-Spirit of Muisca tradition is connected to Nencatacoa, the Muisca god of arts, festivities, and drunkenness who was depicted in the form of a bear or fox and adorned in gold. While Nencatacoa is not primarily a water spirit, his association with the productive forces of nature, celebration, and the creative arts connects him indirectly to the life-giving waters of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, the high plateau near Bogotá where the Muisca civilization flourished. The Muisca were renowned goldsmiths and weavers whose culture centered around the worship of natural forces including the sun, the moon, and the sacred lakes such as Lake Guatavita, the source of the El Dorado legend. In this context, the bear water-spirit represents the generative, creative power of nature that emerges from the union of water and earth, celebrated through the drunken festivals and artistic creations that Nencatacoa oversaw as patron deity of Muisca artists and mantle makers
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of South America, documented in Andean and Amazonian ethnographic records.

name: Bears
description: Bears hold a significant place in Chinook mythology and folklore as powerful beings that appear in the oral traditions of the Chinookan peoples of the Pacific Northwest. The Chinook people, who traditionally inhabited the lower Columbia River region spanning modern-day Washington and Oregon, maintained a rich spiritual tradition in which bears featured as important animal spirits, clan symbols, and characters in mythological narratives. In Chinook cosmology, the natural world is populated by spirits and supernatural beings, and bears were respected for their strength, intelligence, and close relationship with the forest environment. While the Chinook are particularly known for their stories of the trickster Blue Jay and their creation tales involving Thunderbird, bears appear in various narratives as guardians, teachers, and sometimes as adversaries that test the character and courage of human beings who venture into their domain
source: Indigenous North American folklore — bear spirits documented across Native American traditions.

name: Beetgumer Grom
description: The Beetgumer Grom is a ghost from Frisian folklore, specifically from the village of Beetgum, known in Frisian as Bitgum, in the province of Friesland in the Netherlands. This spectral figure is the restless spirit of a murdered farmer who is doomed to haunt the area around Beetgum and the surrounding agricultural lands of the northern Netherlands. Frisian folklore is rich with stories of ghosts and phantoms that reflect the harsh realities of life in the flat, foggy landscape of Friesland, where long winter nights and isolation fostered a strong tradition of supernatural storytelling. The Beetgumer Grom is one of many local ghosts in Friesland whose stories serve as cautionary tales and explanations for unexplained phenomena in the countryside, embodying the Frisian belief that the dead can return to the world of the living when their deaths were violent or their earthly affairs left unresolved
source: Dutch Frisian folklore — Beetgumer Grom ghost documented in Frisian oral tradition.

name: Bell Witch
description: The Bell Witch is the most famous supernatural entity in American folklore, said to have tormented the Bell family of Robertson County, Tennessee, from 1817 to 1821. While white accounts describe the witch as the ghost of Kate Batts, African American oral traditions viewed the Bell Witch through a different lens — as a 'haint' connected to the horrors of slavery itself. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation interpreted the entity as a spirit born from the suffering of the enslaved, and some described it as a Boo Hag-like entity that could shed its skin and fly. The enslaved community used their own protective measures — salt, sulfur, haint blue paint, and conjure bags — to ward off the entity. The Bell Witch legend thus represents a convergence of African and European supernatural traditions on American soil
source: M.V. Ingram, An Authenticated History of the Bell Witch (1894)

name: Belliegħa
description: Belliegħa, also known as Il-Belliegħa, is a female water spirit from Maltese folklore that inhabits wells, springs, and underground water sources across the Maltese islands. In Maltese tradition, which blends ancient Mediterranean beliefs with Christian elements, Belliegħa is a dangerous but fascinating figure who guards the freshwater sources that are precious in the dry Mediterranean climate of Malta. The name Belliegħa is derived from the Maltese word for a swallowing or gulping sound, referencing the way this spirit is said to pull unwary victims into the depths of her watery domain. She belongs to a class of Maltese folk beings that includes the Kawkaw or Gawgaw, a grey slimy creature that roamed the streets at night. Belliegħa embodies both the life-giving and the deadly aspects of water, providing clean drinking water to those who respect her domain but drowning those who approach her wells with carelessness or disrespect
source: Maltese folklore — water spirit documented in Maltese oral tradition.

name: Benandanti
description: Friulian agrarian cult study by Carlo Ginzburg ('The Night Battles') - 'good walkers' who fight malevolent witches (Malandanti) in Spirit Form at night. They Project their spirits (leave body while sleeping) as wolves/cats/hares to battle for crops. The Four Nights per year during Ember Days (Thursdays at specific seasonal times) were key battles - aligned with planting/harvesting. They were NOT werewolves in the usual sense - they Left their human form to go to the 'underworld' to heal the sick, secure paths, fight evil. Their leader was the 'captain.' The Inquisition Reinterpreted them as Satanic witches (1575-1620), forcing confessions. They insisted they fought FOR Christ and against witchcraft. Connect to Livonian 'Dogs of God' werewolves. A PRE-Christian Fertility Cult survivor documented through Inquisition records
source: Friulian folklore; the Benandanti were a secret society of "good walkers" documented by Carlo Ginzburg.

name: Agbé
description: Agbé is the powerful sea deity of the Fon people of Benin, ruling the ocean and all marine life within the Vodun pantheon. As the third-born son of the creator pair Mawu and Lisa, Agbé occupies a crucial position in the divine hierarchy, governing the vast, unpredictable, and life-sustaining waters that border the Fon homeland. For the coastal communities of Benin whose survival depended on fishing and maritime trade, Agbé's presence was immediate and essential. He maintains the delicate balance between water and land, ensuring that the ocean remains a source of nourishment rather than destruction. In Fon cosmology, the earth rests upon primordial waters, making Agbé not just a sea god but a stabilizing force beneath the world itself. His role extends to controlling tides, currents, storms, and marine life. Agbé's worship has been carried across the Atlantic through the slave trade, where he became Agwé in Haitian Vodou, retaining his identity as lord of the sea depicted as a regal figure associated with ships and ocean travel
source: Fon oral tradition and Vodun religious practice

name: Aziza
description: The Aziza are benevolent forest spirits in Fon and Dahomean mythology of Benin. Described as diminutive 'little people,' these beings inhabit anthills, hollow trees, and sacred groves within the deep forests. Unlike many spirits in West African folklore that are feared, the Aziza are known for their wisdom and generosity toward humans who respect the forest. They are credited with teaching humanity essential survival skills including the use of fire, knowledge of medicinal herbs, hunting techniques, and tracking of animals. The Aziza serve as moral arbiters of the forest, providing guidance and assistance to those who show proper respect for nature while withholding help from those who violate ethical or ecological boundaries. In their original pre-contact form, the Aziza were wingless little people; later European-influenced accounts sometimes depict them with butterfly-like wings, though this is considered a syncretic addition. They represent the Fon worldview that wisdom and survival knowledge originate from respectful engagement with the natural world
source: Wikipedia, Dahomean Religion summaries

name: Legba
description: Legba is the trickster god and divine intermediary in Fon Vodun cosmology of Benin, serving as the essential gatekeeper who opens communication between the human and spirit worlds. No ceremony, prayer, or offering can reach the other Vodun deities without Legba's permission and assistance. He stands at the cosmic crossroads, speaking all human languages, and is the master of doors, pathways, and communication. Legba is a complex figure with both benevolent and malevolent aspects — he can facilitate blessings or create obstacles depending on how he is approached. He is typically depicted as an old man with a walking cane or crutch, wearing a broad-brimmed straw hat and smoking a pipe. Legba is the first spirit invoked at the beginning of every Vodun ceremony, and his role has been carried to the Americas through the slave trade, becoming Papa Legba in Haitian Vodou and Exu in Brazilian Candomblé. Dogs are sacred to Legba, and his offerings include candy, tobacco, and coffee
source: Fon oral tradition and Vodun religious practice

name: Bergfolk
description: Bergfolk (mountain-people) are supernatural beings in Norwegian folklore who live inside mountains and rocky crags. Similar to haugfolk but specifically associated with mountains rather than burial mounds. Bergfolk are a type of underjordiske (hidden people) who have their own society within mountain halls. They are known for kidnapping humans (bergtaking - mountain-taking), where a person would be taken inside the mountain to live with the bergfolk, often for years. The most famous example is the legend of the Huldra who entices men into the mountain. Time is distorted inside - a few hours can be years in the human world. Bergfolk have beautiful daughters who sometimes marry human men. The mountain halls are lit by an internal golden light and filled with treasure. The theme of bergtaking (entering the mountain and being trapped) is central to Norwegian folklore and appears in Asbjørnsen and Moe's collections
source: Norwegian folklore, collected by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe

name: Bergkobold
description: The Bergkobold is a mine spirit from German folklore, particularly associated with the Harz Mountains, the Ore Mountains of Saxony, and other mining regions of central Europe. Unlike the household kobold, which helps with domestic chores, the Bergkobold or mountain kobold inhabits underground mines and tunnels, where it can be either helpful or dangerous to miners depending on how it is treated. In German mining tradition, which dates back to the Middle Ages, these spirits were believed to inhabit the rich veins of silver, copper, tin, and cobalt that drew generations of miners into the mountains. The connection between kobolds and mining is so strong that the element cobalt derives its name from the German word kobold, because the cobalt ore was considered worthless and was believed to be placed in the mines by mischievous kobolds to fool and frustrate miners. The Bergkobold represents the inherent danger and uncertainty of mining, the thin line between striking it rich and losing everything in a cave-in or flood
source: Germany mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Betal
description: A vampiric undead being from Indian folklore, particularly prominent in the Konkan region of Goa and Maharashtra. The Betal is a complex figure that hangs upside down from trees near cremation grounds and ancient battlefields, guarding occult knowledge and secrets of the dead. Unlike common ghosts, the Betal possesses a cunning intelligence and delights in riddles and philosophical debates. It is known to test the bravery and wisdom of those who dare approach it, sometimes rewarding clever individuals with supernatural gifts or hidden truths about the universe. The Betal is deeply tied to death rituals and is said to be unable to cross consecrated ground or enter spaces protected by proper funeral rites. In the famous Vikram-Vetala tales, King Vikramaditya must capture a Betal and engage in a series of riddle contests that reveal profound moral lessons about duty, honor, and the nature of reality
source: India mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Betobeto-san
description: A Japanese yokai or supernatural entity from Nara and Shizuoka prefectures that manifests as an invisible presence following people who walk alone at night. Betobeto-san is one of the more benign yokai in Japanese folklore, causing no direct physical harm but creating an unsettling sense of being stalked through the darkness. The creature is said to prefer dark, rural roads and mountain paths, where its victims become aware of disembodied footsteps echoing behind them. The name Betobeto-san is onomatopoeic, deriving from the sticky or tacky sound of footsteps on a path. According to traditional belief, the correct response when hearing these footsteps is to step aside and politely say Go ahead, Betobeto-san, allowing the invisible being to pass. The yokai is deeply connected to the Japanese folk tradition of unseen spirits that inhabit the boundaries between the human world and the spirit realm
source: Japanese folklore; an invisible spirit that follows people at night.

name: Bhand
description: A vengeful ghost or malevolent spirit from Indian folklore, particularly known in the northern regions of the Indian subcontinent. The Bhand is believed to be the restless soul of a person who died through violence, betrayal, or under circumstances that left their final desires unfulfilled. Unlike the more common Bhoot, the Bhand is specifically associated with unfinished business and a deep-seated rage that prevents the spirit from moving on to the afterlife. These spirits are said to haunt the locations of their deaths, appearing to those who remind them of their former lives or to individuals who inadvertently trespass on their territory. Traditional accounts describe the Bhand as a trickster spirit that delights in leading travelers astray, hiding objects, and creating confusing illusions in the darkness. The spirit is particularly active during the night and is said to draw power from fear and strong negative emotions
source: Pakistan mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bhoot
description: A ghost or disembodied spirit of a deceased person in the folklore of the Indian subcontinent, deeply embedded in Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist cultural traditions across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. Bhoots are believed to be the souls of individuals who died premature or violent deaths, were denied proper funeral rites, or left unresolved matters in their lives. Unlike the souls that successfully transmigrate, bhoots remain trapped in the mortal realm, often haunting specific locations connected to their deaths. The belief in bhoots has existed for thousands of years and is referenced in ancient texts including the Garuda Purana, which provides detailed instructions for dealing with these spirits. Bhoots occupy a significant place in South Asian popular culture, appearing in countless films, television shows, and folk tales that explore the boundary between the living and the dead
source: Myanmar mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bhoot of Haveli
description: A specific type of Indian ghost that haunts large ancestral mansions known as havelis, characteristic of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh. The Bhoot of Haveli is the restless spirit of a former resident who died tragically within the walls of the grand family home, often due to family feuds, betrayal, poisoning, or the violent politics of noble households. These spirits are deeply tied to the architecture and history of the haveli itself, becoming part of the fabric of the building. Havelis were traditionally built around central courtyards with intricate frescoes, secret passages, and multiple stories that provided countless hiding places for secrets and tragedies. The folklore surrounding these haunted mansions has been a staple of South Asian horror literature and cinema, with many famous havelis across the region earning reputations as genuinely haunted locations where the boundary between past and present grows thin after dark
source: Pakistan mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bhuta
description: A supernatural creature and restless ghost from the Indian subcontinent, deeply rooted in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions that span thousands of years. The Bhuta is the spirit of a deceased person who, due to a violent death, unfulfilled desires, improper funeral rites, or unfinished earthly business, remains trapped between worlds instead of proceeding to the afterlife or reincarnation. The concept of Bhuta encompasses a wide spectrum of supernatural beings, from genuinely malevolent spirits that actively seek to harm the living to confused entities simply trying to communicate their needs. Bhuta belief is particularly strong in South India, where the Bhuta Kola ritual tradition involves elaborate spirit possession ceremonies conducted by trained priests. These spirits are believed to have the power to influence the lives of the living, both positively when propitiated and negatively when angered or ignored
source: India mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bieggolmmái
description: Bieggolmmái (the Wind Man) is the Sami god of wind and weather, one of the most important deities for reindeer herding and fishing peoples of Sapmi. He lives in a cave and holds two shovels — with one he releases wind from his cave, with the other he puts it back. According to the Nærøy manuscript, he had a shovel in his right hand to scoop wind back into his caves after it had blown enough, and a club in his left hand to chase the wind back out when needed. He was crucial for reindeer herding because reindeer travel into headwinds to avoid mosquitoes. A single wind direction persisting too long could drive reindeer far away, requiring a sacrifice — preferably a white reindeer — to Bieggolmmái. Some sources distinguish between Bieggolmmái (summer wind god) and Gissenolmmái (winter wind god who ruled over snow and ice). Tiny birch-bark boats with offerings were set adrift as sacrifices. The Inari Sami sacrificed to him at Piegg-oaivadz fells (the Heads of the Winds)
source: Wikipedia (Bieggolmai); saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; heimskringla.no; grandma-in-lapland.com

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: A revered ancestral spirit from Kwakwakaawakw (Kwakiutl) mythology of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America, representing the sacred bison as a symbol of strength, abundance, and spiritual power. In Kwakwakaawakw tradition, animal spirits are not separate from human society but are considered ancestors, teachers, and clan founders who bestowed their spiritual treasures upon human families at the beginning of time. The bison, though not native to the coastal rainforest environment of the Kwakwakaawakw, is known through trade and cultural exchange with Plains nations and is incorporated into the spiritual cosmology as a symbol of the vast power of the natural world. These ancestor-spirits are central to the potlatch ceremony system, where their stories, songs, and dances are performed as inherited privileges that validate the status of noble families within the complex social hierarchy
source: Pacific Northwest indigenous folklore, oral traditions

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Aztec
description: An animal spirit from Aztec mythology representing the bison as a symbolic figure of strength, fertility, and the life-giving power of the earth. In Aztec cosmology, the natural world was populated by a vast array of spirits and supernatural forces that governed every aspect of existence. The bison, known to the Aztecs through trade networks that extended far north of the Valley of Mexico, was recognized as a powerful creature embodying the raw vitality of the wilderness. Aztec animal spirits were often associated with specific deities, calendar days, and ritual practices. They served as tonal animal companions that shared a spiritual bond with human beings from birth, influencing their character and destiny. The bison spirit was particularly associated with warriors and hunters, representing the courage and physical power required to face the challenges of the natural and supernatural worlds
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Quechua
description: An animal spirit from Quechua mythology of the Andean region, representing the bison as a symbol of strength, abundance, and the wild vitality of the natural world. The Quechua people, descendants of the Inca civilization, maintain a rich spiritual tradition in which the natural landscape is inhabited by powerful spirits known as apus and huacas that govern the forces of nature and the well-being of human communities. The bison, while more commonly associated with the North American plains, was known in parts of South America and appears in Andean cosmology as a representation of untamed power. In Quechua tradition, animal spirits are considered teachers and guides that reveal the proper way to live in harmony with the earth. The relationship between humans and animal spirits is one of mutual respect, with offerings and rituals maintaining the sacred balance between the human and natural worlds
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of South America, documented in Andean and Amazonian ethnographic records.

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Yurok
description: An animal spirit from Yurok mythology of Northern California, representing the bison as a figure of spiritual power and abundance despite the bison not being native to the Yurok coastal territory. The Yurok people traditionally inhabited the lower Klamath River region, where their spiritual cosmology centers around the balance between the river, the ocean, the forest, and the sky. Animal spirits in Yurok tradition are powerful beings that established the proper way of doing things during the time of the Immortals, before the world was fully formed. These spirits taught the first humans how to conduct ceremonies, build houses, and maintain the social and spiritual order. The bison, known through trade and cultural exchange with interior tribes, represents the vast interior world beyond the coastal redwood forests and is incorporated into Yurok cosmology as a symbol of the broader web of relationships that connect all Native peoples
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Bison Deity of Baloch
description: The Bison Deity of Baloch is a sacred water buffalo spirit revered by the Baloch people of Pakistan and Iran. In Balochi cosmology, this powerful bovine deity is associated with water sources, fertility, and pastoral prosperity, reflecting the central role of livestock in traditional Baloch nomadic culture. The deity governs the seasonal migrations of herds and ensures that springs and rivers continue to flow through the arid Balochistan landscape, where water is the most precious resource. Local legends describe this being as an ancient guardian who emerged from the Hingol River during a time of great drought, teaching the ancestors how to find water by following wild buffalo tracks across the desert. Devotees still pour milk into rivers as offerings and tie prayer ribbons at sacred waterholes believed to be visited by the deity during the spring equinox
source: Central Asian folklore, Turkic & Mongol oral traditions

name: Bison Deity of Choctaw
description: The Bison Deity of the Choctaw people is an ancient buffalo spirit that holds a central place in Choctaw creation narratives and agricultural traditions. Choctaw oral history tells of the Great Buffalo who emerged from the sacred mound Nanih Waiya alongside the first Choctaw ancestors, offering its flesh for sustenance and its thick hide for shelter during the people's long migration from the west. Unlike the hunting-focused bison spirits of Plains tribes, the Choctaw Bison Deity is primarily an agricultural and domestic figure, associated with the bounty of the earth and the cycle of planting and harvest. Tribal elders recount that the deity taught the Choctaw how to use every part of the buffalo without waste, and that its spirit still runs through the tallgrass prairies of Mississippi and Oklahoma, appearing to those who maintain the old ways of gratitude before the hunt
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Bison Ghost of Lakota
description: The Bison Ghost of Lakota is a spectral buffalo spirit that haunts the Black Hills and the Great Plains, embodying the collective soul of the vast herds that once sustained the Lakota people. Unlike living buffalo, this ghostly manifestation is the spiritual residue of the ancient buffalo nation that has passed into the spirit world, serving as a bridge between the physical realm and the domain of Wakan Tanka. In Lakota tradition, the Bison Ghost appears as an omen of great change, either heralding times of abundance and renewal or warning of coming hardship depending on the direction from which it approaches. Some elders say that when the last white buffalo calf is born, the Bison Ghost will lead the ancestral herds back across the plains from the spirit world, ushering in an era of healing and restoration for the Lakota people and the return of the sacred hoop
source: Lakota spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous ethnographic records.

name: Bison Giant of Lakota
description: The Bison Giant of Lakota is a primordial titan from the age when the Great Plains were first being shaped, a colossal buffalo being whose steps carved the river valleys and whose sleeping body formed the Black Hills. Known in Lakota oral tradition as the first and largest of all buffalo, this giant walked the earth before the coming of humans, when only the stone people and the star people existed. The Bison Giant is closely associated with the White Buffalo Calf Woman narrative, as some versions of the story describe it as the source from which the sacred pipe's bowl was quarried, the red pipestone being the fossilized blood of the ancient giant. When the Bison Giant finally lay down to rest, its body became the rolling prairies, its hide became the tallgrass, and its spirit splintered into the countless buffalo that would later sustain the Lakota and other Plains nations
source: Lakota spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous ethnographic records.

name: Bison Giant of Mapuche
description: The Bison Giant of Mapuche tradition is an enormous supernatural bovine being from the mythology of the Mapuche people of Chile and Argentina. While true bison are not native to South America, the Mapuche cosmology describes a giant horned creature related to the wild cattle and guanaco that roamed the Andean foothills before the arrival of Europeans. This primordial being is linked to the Pillan, the powerful ancestral spirits that reside within volcanoes and control the forces of nature. The Bison Giant is said to live inside the Osorno and Villarrica volcanoes, emerging during times of great upheaval when the balance between Wenu Mapu (the sky world) and Nag Mapu (the earth world) is threatened. Oral traditions describe it as one of the ancient animal spirits that the machi shamans call upon during the Nguillatun ceremony to restore harmony to the land
source: Mapuche folklore — bison giant from Chilean oral tradition.

name: Bison Nature-Spirit (Aztec)
description: The Bison Nature-Spirit in Aztec tradition is a syncretic earth spirit that emerged from the blending of Mesoamerican nature worship with European cattle symbolism introduced after contact. In the Aztec worldview, the natural world was filled with tlaloqueh, minor rain and earth spirits who served the great gods and maintained the fertility of the land. This bison spirit belongs to that class of nature beings, acting as a guardian of the grasslands and a mediator between the agricultural cycles of humans and the wild forces of the earth. It is associated with Xipe Totec, the flayed god of spring and new vegetation, as the bison's shedding of its winter coat mirrors the renewal of life that comes with the planting season. The spirit teaches that the health of the land and the health of the people are inseparable, and that proper stewardship of the earth requires both ritual devotion and practical care
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Bison Nature-Spirit of Zapotec
description: The Bison Nature-Spirit of the Zapotec people is a pre-Columbian earth spirit from the Oaxaca region of Mexico, adapted from the worship of bovine-like deities that existed in Zapotec religion before and after European contact. In Zapotec cosmology, the natural world was inhabited by a class of spirits called pitao, who governed the forces of nature and the fertility of the land. This bison spirit is considered a pitao of the grasslands and wild grains, responsible for the health of the uncultivated lands that surround Zapotec villages. The spirit is particularly associated with the mountain shrines where the Zapotec made offerings to ensure good harvests and the well-being of their communities. Despite the absence of true bison in pre-Columbian Oaxaca, the spirit represents the bovine principle that was later recognized and named when cattle and bison became known to the Zapotec through trade and colonization
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Bison Spirit of Aztec
description: The Bison Spirit of Aztec tradition is a syncretic earth spirit that emerged after European contact when Mesoamerican peoples encountered cattle and bison through Spanish colonizers and later through trade with northern indigenous nations. In the Aztec cosmological framework, which organizes all beings into a complex system of symbolic associations, the bison was integrated as a creature of the west, the direction of the color white, the plant maize, and the goddess Chicomecoatl, the seven-serpent goddess of agricultural sustenance. This spirit belongs to the class of earth-bound beings that serve the greater gods by maintaining the fertility of the soil and the abundance of game. It is a spirit of the teotl sacred force, manifesting in the material world as a reminder that survival depends on respect for the cycles of nature that sustain human life. The spirit gained particular importance in communities that relied on cattle for plowing and transport
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Bison Trickster of Creek
description: The Bison Trickster of the Creek (Muscogee) people is a shape-shifting guardian spirit that presides over the swamplands and river deltas of the southeastern United States, a region where water and land intermingle in vast cypress wetlands. Unlike the plains bison spirits of western tribes, this entity has adapted to the humid, waterlogged environment of the Creek homelands, becoming a creature equally at home in water and on land. The Bison Trickster is known among the Creek people as a teacher of hard lessons—it appears to those who have grown arrogant or careless, using elaborate tricks and illusions to humble them. Its connection to the swamps gives it dominion over the threshold between solid earth and murky water, making it a spirit of boundaries, transitions, and the liminal spaces where rules change. Elders teach that the Bison Trickster's pranks carry warnings about the consequences of disrespecting nature, community, and tradition
source: USA mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bison Trickster of Quechua
description: The Bison Trickster of the Quechua people is a high-altitude spirit that governs the skies and mountain peaks of the Peruvian Andes, a realm where bison are not native but where the spirit has adapted to embody the wild, untamed energy of the puna grasslands and the sacred mountain peaks. This entity is associated with lightning, thunder, and the sudden storms that sweep across the altiplano without warning. In Quechua cosmology, the Bison Trickster represents the chaotic and unpredictable forces of nature that exist above the tree line, where only the hardiest creatures and spirits dwell. It is neither benevolent nor malevolent but operates according to its own inscrutable logic, testing the courage and wisdom of those who venture into the high country. The spirit is particularly associated with the concept of pachakuti—a world-turning or upheaval—and its appearances are said to herald times of change, challenge, and transformation for individuals and communities alike
source: Peru mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bison Trickster of Shona
description: The Bison Trickster of the Shona people is a mountain-dwelling spirit that inhabits the granite kopjes and rocky highlands of Zimbabwe, serving as the guardian of the sacred hills where the ancestors dwell. In Shona cosmology, mountains are liminal spaces where the physical and spiritual worlds meet, and the Bison Trickster is the gatekeeper of these thresholds. It is a shape-shifting entity that appears to those who venture into the mountains without proper respect, leading them astray with clever illusions and echoes that seem to come from all directions at once. The Bison Trickster is particularly associated with the Mwari cult, the traditional Shona religious system, and is considered a messenger between the high god Mwari and the human world. Its lessons are harsh but never fatal—the spirit always leaves a path to redemption for those who recognize their mistakes and approach the mountains with genuine humility and reverence for the ancestors who rest within them
source: Zimbabwe mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bison Water-Spirit of Dogon
description: The Bison Water-Spirit of the Dogon people is a sacred spring guardian that dwells in the hidden water sources of the Bandiagara Escarpment in Mali, a region where water is precious and springs are considered living entities with their own spirits. In Dogon cosmology, springs are the mouths of the underworld, connecting the surface world to the waters of the ancestors below, and the Bison Water-Spirit is the keeper of these sacred portals. The Dogon people, renowned for their sophisticated astronomical knowledge and complex mythology, regard this spirit as an essential part of their creation narratives. It is said that the Nommo—the ancestral water spirits who created the world—placed the Bison Water-Spirit at each major spring to guard the balance between the water that gives life and the water that can take it away. The spirit's presence ensures that the springs flow steadily throughout the year, and its anger is believed to be the cause of sudden droughts or the mysterious drying up of previously reliable water sources
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Bison Water-Spirit of Maya
description: The Bison Water-Spirit of the Maya people is a vast oceanic entity that presides over the Caribbean and Pacific waters surrounding Guatemala and the Yucatán Peninsula, a spirit born from the fusion of Maya water mythology with the symbolism of the bison. In Maya cosmology, water is the primordial substance from which all life emerged, and the great sea is both the source of creation and the realm of chaos. This water-spirit embodies that duality, appearing as a bison made of ocean energy that rises from the depths during storms and great celestial events. The Maya associated the bison with strength, endurance, and the cyclical nature of life—qualities that map perfectly onto their understanding of the ocean's moods. The Bison Water-Spirit is particularly associated with Chaac, the Maya rain god, and is sometimes described as Chaac's aquatic steed or messenger. Its appearances are tied to the movements of Venus, the cycles of the rainy season, and the great calendar rounds that structure Maya spiritual life
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Bizango (Haitian Secret Society Spirits)
description: Bizango refers to both a powerful class of Petwo lwa (spirits) in Haitian Vodou and the secret societies that serve them. These are the most feared and potent spirits in the Vodou pantheon -- considered maximum Petro -- associated with skulls, coffins, crosses, and crucifixes. The Bizango spirits include formidable entities such as Baron Kriminel and Ezili Zandor. The Bizango secret societies trace their origins to the Maroons -- escaped slaves who resisted colonial rule from Haiti mountains. Their colors are red and black. They are reputed to serve as social enforcers within Vodou communities, administering justice, settling disputes, and punishing those who violate community codes. The most notorious aspect of Bizango practice is the creation of zombis -- using neurotoxic poisons (typically from pufferfish and other sources) to induce a catatonic state, then reviving the victim to serve as a laborer. Members are feared for their ability to shape-shift into dogs, cats, or other animals to walk the streets at night undetected
source: Haitian Vodou oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Black Rocks Mermaids
description: The Black Rocks Mermaids are vengeful and cunning sea spirits that inhabit the waters off Black Rocks, a rugged expanse of volcanic rock formations on the northeastern coast of St. Unlike the gentle mermaids of other cultures, these are dangerous sirens who lure unsuspecting sailors to their doom with enchanting songs and mesmerizing beauty. According to legend, a group of fishermen enticed by the siren call ventured too close to the rocks and disappeared without a trace, never to be seen again. Some Kittitians believe the mermaids are protectors of the island who ensure only those who respect the sea can traverse its waters safely. The volcanic rock formations at Black Rocks were created by ancient volcanic activity from Mount Liamuiga, adding a geological dimension to the supernatural legend
source: St. Kitts and Nevis oral tradition; snip StKittsNevis.net

name: Blak
description: Blak is a colossal pike spirit from Finnish mythology, a primordial fish entity that dwells in the deepest, darkest lakes of the Finnish lake district, particularly those connected to the mythology of Ahti, the god of waters. In Finnish folklore, the Blak is more than a mere giant fish—it is an ancient, semi-divine being that predates the arrival of humans in the northern forests. The creature is intimately connected with the Finnish national epic, the Kalevala, where the hero Väinämöinen creates the first kantele (the Finnish stringed instrument) from the jawbone of a giant pike, an act that brings music and poetry into the world. The Blak represents the untamed, mysterious depths of the Finnish wilderness—the shadowy, unknown waters that hide secrets from the rational world. It is both a physical creature and a spiritual entity, capable of interacting with humans as either a fish, a spirit, or a shape-shifted human, depending on its mood and the circumstances of the encounter
source: Finnish mythology, Kalevala compiled by Elias Lönnrot

name: Bluecap
description: The English Bluecap is a mine spirit from the coal mining regions of northern England, particularly Northumberland and Durham, where it has been a fixture of mining folklore for centuries. Like its Scottish cousin, the English Bluecap is a helpful household spirit of the mines, but English traditions emphasize its role as a supernatural putter—a worker who pushes heavy coal tubs along underground tramways with seemingly impossible strength. The English Bluecap is considered a distinct yet related entity to the Scottish Bluecap, shaped by the specific conditions of English coal mines where narrow seams and long tunnels made the work of putters particularly arduous. Miners regard the Bluecap with a mixture of familiarity and respect, treating it more as an unusual coworker than a supernatural being. The tradition of leaving wages for the Bluecap is taken seriously in English mining communities, and stories are told of mines that prospered or failed based on how well the resident Bluecap was treated. The English Bluecap lacks the fairy-like qualities of its Scottish counterpart, instead appearing as a more industrial spirit adapted to the harsh environment of deep coal mining In England folklore, this figure is known among the England people.
source: England mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

source: Scottish folklore, collected by John Francis Campbell

name: Bodu Naga (Maldivian Sea Serpent)
description: Bodu Naga is a great serpent spirit in Maldivian folklore that inhabits lagoons, reefs, and deep channels between the Maldivian atolls. The name means 'Great Serpent' in Divehi (Bodu = big/great, Naga = serpent). In pre-Islamic Maldives, nagas were revered as powerful nature spirits associated with the waters that surrounded the atolls. Bodu Naga is described as a guardian of the sea, protecting certain channels, passes, and reefs. Fishermen offered prayers and small offerings before venturing into waters believed to be guarded by Bodu Naga to ensure safe passage and abundant catch. The entity is part of a broader Maldivian tradition of spirit beings (handi, fureytha, dhevi, and fan'du) that could appear in human form — often as beautiful women or well-built men — to lure humans into danger. Bodu Naga reflects the ancient Dravidian naga worship that existed in the Maldives before the advent of Buddhism and later Islam, sharing similarities with serpent traditions across South India and Sri Lanka. The nagas were said to have been subdued as Buddhism spread through the Indian Ocean, but their stories persist in folklore about dangerous waters and forbidden reefs
source: Xavier Romero-Frias 'Folk Tales of the Maldives', Maldivian oral maritime tradition

name: Boginka
description: Boginka is a female nature spirit from Slavic mythology, particularly prominent in Polish folklore, where she inhabits forests, fields, lakes, and rivers. The name 'Boginka' derives from 'bóg' meaning god, positioning these spirits as minor goddesses or divine feminine entities of the natural world. Boginki are complex beings that defy simple categorization—they can appear as beautiful young women who enchant travelers or as hideous old hags who terrify those who cross them. This dual nature reflects the Slavic understanding of nature itself as both nurturing and dangerous, beautiful and terrifying. Boginki are closely related to the more widely known Rusalki, but while Rusalki are specifically the spirits of drowned maidens, Boginki are a broader category of nature spirits that include water spirits, forest spirits, and field spirits. In Polish folklore, Boginki are particularly associated with the protection of wild animals and plants, and they punish those who hunt for sport, pick plants without asking permission, or otherwise disrespect the natural order. Despite their dangerous reputation, Boginki can be benevolent to those who show proper respect, sometimes granting blessings of fertility, good harvests, or protection from misfortune
source: Polish folklore — Boginka spirit documented in Polish oral tradition.

name: Boiadeira
description: Boiadeira, also known as Boiúna or the Great Black Serpent of the Amazon, is a fearsome water spirit from Brazilian folklore, particularly associated with the Amazon River basin and the vast network of tributaries that flow through the rainforest. The name 'Boiadeira' derives from 'boia' (a type of snake) or possibly from 'boi' (ox), reflecting the creature's dual nature as both serpent and bull-like river monster. Boiadeira is one of the most feared entities in Amazonian folklore, described as a colossal black serpent with eyes like fire that glows in the darkness of the river at night. It is said to be the guardian of the Amazon's deepest waters, protecting the secrets and treasures that lie beneath the surface. The creature is particularly notorious for capsizing fishing boats, dragging fishermen to their deaths, and devouring anyone foolish enough to swim in its territory after dark. In some traditions, Boiadeira is associated with the Yacumama (Mother of the Waters) and is considered the female counterpart to the male river spirit, the Cobra Grande. Despite its fearsome reputation, Boiadeira is not purely malevolent—it enforces ecological balance in the rivers, punishing those who overfish or pollute the waters
source: Brazilian folklore — the Boiadeira ox-ogre documented by Câmara Cascudo.

name: Boitatá
description: Boitatá is a legendary fire serpent from Brazilian folklore, deeply rooted in the mythology of the Tupi-Guarani indigenous people and later incorporated into broader Brazilian folk tradition. The name 'Boitatá' comes from the Tupi words 'mboi' (snake) and 'tata' (fire), literally meaning 'fire snake.' Boitatá is a protector spirit of the forests and fields, particularly active during the dry season when wildfires are most common. According to legend, Boitatá was once a giant, blind serpent that survived a great flood by crawling into a hollow log. When the waters receded, the serpent emerged with its eyes damaged by darkness but gained the power to see through fire, developing a body that glowed like living flame. The creature now patrols the wilderness, devouring the ashes of burned areas and consuming the rotting remains of dead animals to return their nutrients to the earth. Boitatá is fundamentally a benevolent entity focused on environmental renewal, using its fiery body to burn away decay and make way for new growth. However, its fiery nature makes it dangerous to humans who approach too closely or threaten the forests it protects
source: Tupi-Guarani mythology; the Boitatá is a giant fiery serpent that protects the forest.
